source_text: Ἐξαιτοῦμαι δὲ παρά τε φιλοσόφων τῶν νῦν ὄντων, ὅσους αὐτὸς ἔγνων, καὶ ὅσους ἄλλων διηγουμένων ἤκουσα, καὶ παρὰ τῶν ἄλλων δὲ ἀνθρώπων, ἀνεμεσήτως ἔχειν πρὸς τὰ νῦν ἡμῖν λεγόμενα. μηδέ με τις ἢ φιλίᾳ τῇ πρὸς τὸν ἄνδρα, ἢ καὶ ἀπεχθανόμενον ἔτι τοῖς λοιποῖς φιλοσόφοις (ὧν, εἴπερ τις ἄλλος, καὶ αὐτὸς ἐραστής τε διὰ τοὺς λόγους εἶναι θέλω, καὶ εὐφημεῖν αὐτοὺς βούλομαι, αὐτός τε καὶ ἑτέρων τὰ μάλιστα λεγόντων περὶ αὐτῶν ἀκούειν· ἀλλὰ γὰρ τοιαῦτά ἐστιν, ὡς εἰς ἔσχατον περιυβρίζεσθαι μὲν ὑπὸ πάντων σχεδὸν καὶ τοὔνομα τῆς φιλοσοφίας, ἐμὲ δὲ μικροῦ δεῖν ἰδιωτεύειν ἑλέσθαι πάντῃ, ἤπερ τι μαθεῖν ὧν οὗτοι ἀπαγγέλλουσιν, οἷς διὰ τὸν λοιπὸν βίον οὐδὲ προσιέναι ἄξιον εἶναι ἐδόκουν, ἴσως οὐκ ὀρθῶς τοῦτο φρονῶν)· πλὴν μή μέ τις φιλοτιμίᾳ τινί, ἤτοι τῶν εἰς τὸν ἄνδρα ἐπαίνων, ἢ τῇ πρὸς τοὺς ἔξω φιλοσόφους ἄλλῃ ταύτῃ φιλοτιμίᾳ ταῦτα λέγειν ὑπονοησάτω· ἀλλὰ καὶ μικρότερα ἡμᾶς τῶν αὐτοῦ ἔργων, μὴ κολακεύειν δοκοίημεν, λέγειν πεπείσθω· οὐχὶ ῥήματα καὶ ὀνόματα, καὶ ἀφορμὰς ἐντέχνους ἐγκωμίων ἑαυτοῖς ἐκποριζομένοις, ὃς οὐδ' ὅτε μειράκιον ὤν, τὴν δημώδη ῥητορικὴν ἐκ ῥήτορος ἐδιδασκόμην, ἐπαινεῖν, καὶ λέγειν περί του ἐγκώμιον, ὅ,τι μὴ ἀληθὲς ἦν, ἑκὼν ὑπέμενον. οὐ τοίνυν οὐδὲ νῦν ἐπαινεῖν προθέμενος, ἁπλῶς τοῖς ἑτέρων ψόγοις τοῦτον ἐξαίρειν οἶμαι δεῖν· ἢ κακῶς ἂν ἔλεγον τὸν ἄνδρα, τοῖς ἄλλων πταίσμασιν, ἵνα τι περὶ αὐτοῦ μεῖζον δὴ λέγειν ἔχοιμι, παραβαλὼν τὸν μακάριον αὐτοῦ βίον. οὐχ οὕτως ἀφραίνομεν· ἀλλ' αὐτὸ ὃ πέπονθα δίχα τινὸς παραβολῆς καὶ πανουργίας τῆς ἐν λόγοις, ὁμολογήσω.
thought_title: A plea to the philosophers before the praise
orientation: Gregory asks the other philosophers not to take offense at his praise of Origen.
pass_a_gloss: I beg from the philosophers now being, as many as I myself knew, and as many as I heard of from others relating, and from the other men, to be without indignation toward the things now said by us. Nor [let] anyone [think] me either by friendship toward the man, or also still being hostile to the remaining philosophers (of whom, if anyone else, I myself also wish to be a lover because of their words/teachings, and wish to speak well of them, myself and to hear others speaking most about them; but they are such that the very name of philosophy is outraged to the extreme by almost all, and that I nearly chose to be wholly a layman rather than learn anything of what these announce, whom because of the rest of their life I thought it not worthy even to approach, perhaps not thinking this rightly) — but let no one suspect me to say these things from some ambition, either of praises toward the man, or by this other ambition toward the outside philosophers; but let him be persuaded that we say things even smaller than his works, lest we seem to flatter; not procuring for ourselves phrases and names and artful starting-points of encomia — I who not even when being a youth, learning popular rhetoric from a rhetor, would willingly endure to praise and to speak an encomium about anyone what was not true. Not then now either, having set out to praise, do I think it necessary simply to exalt this man by the blames of others; or I would speak badly of the man, by the stumbles of others, so that I might have something greater to say about him, comparing his blessed life. We are not so senseless; but the very thing I have experienced, without any comparison and knavery in words, I will confess.

pass_b_english: I ask the philosophers of our day, both those I have known myself and those I have heard of from others, and everyone else as well, not to take offense at what I am now saying. Let no one think I say this out of friendship for the man, or else out of hostility toward the other philosophers. As much as anyone, I wish to be a devoted lover of them for the sake of their teachings; I want to speak well of them myself, and to hear others speak most highly of them. But their ways are such that the very name of philosophy is insulted to the last degree by nearly everyone, and I very nearly chose to stay wholly untaught rather than learn any of the things these men teach; for because of the rest of their lives I did not think them worth even approaching, though perhaps I did not judge rightly in this. So, I say, let no one suspect that I speak from some ambition, either in praising the man or in that other rivalry against the philosophers outside. Let him rather be assured that, so as not to seem to flatter, we are saying less than his deeds deserve. We are not supplying ourselves with phrases and words and the stock devices of the art for a eulogy. Even as a youth, when I was learning popular rhetoric from a rhetorician, I would not willingly bring myself to say anything untrue in praising anyone or in speaking a eulogy about anyone. Nor now, then, when I have set out to praise, do I think I should simply raise this man up by blaming others. Otherwise I would be speaking ill of him, setting his blessed life beside other people’s failings so as to have something greater to say about him. We are not so foolish. Instead I will confess exactly what happened to me, without comparisons or verbal trickery.
notes: Copy-text: Greek column of the 1622 Paris Opera omnia (printed p. 66), as in the source row. The sentence begun with μηδέ με τις … is broken by the long parenthesis (ὧν … φρονῶν) and resumed with πλὴν μή μέ τις … ὑπονοησάτω; Pass B supplies ‘think I say this’ in the first limb from the resumed verb. τὰ μάλιστα λεγόντων follows the print (Koetschau, from A, τὰ κάλλιστα, ‘speak most finely of them’); rendered ‘speak most highly of them’, the sense the context of εὐφημεῖν requires. τοιαῦτά ἐστιν is taken of the philosophers’ conduct (‘their ways are such’), in line with ‘because of the rest of their lives’ and with the facing Latin of the 1622 print (haec illorum talia sunt). ἔτι with ἀπεχθανόμενον is rendered ‘or else’; ‘lingering’ would claim an earlier hostility the Greek does not state. οἱ ἔξω φιλόσοφοι, ‘the philosophers outside’, is kept literal; it means philosophers outside Origen’s circle. The dative participle ἐκποριζομένοις has no expressed noun; it is taken with ‘we’. No Scripture in this section.
